name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Sunday 19 November 1989

clue.text: Paul gone to Tassie to spoon? Some blade!

indicators.note: something gone astray is out of place, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: Tassie is Australian slang for Tasmania, whose standard abbreviation is TAS

explanation.surface: Paul heads to Tasmania to canoodle, quite the dashing young man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blade' looks like the old word for a dashing young man; it is a flat implement. Tassie is Tasmania, the island state of Australia.
explanation.definitionFit: A spatula has a broad flat blade for lifting or spreading, a spoon-like kitchen utensil.

clue.text: To excavate, use fingers and toes!

definitions.note: plural, while the answer is a single finger or toe

blocks.clueFragment: To excavate, use fingers and toes!
blocks.note: surface reading: advice to dig with your hands and feet
setter's reading: an order to excavate something, two short words that run together into a body-part word

explanation.surface: Advice to dig with your bare hands and feet.
explanation.walkthrough: The pun is that 'dig it' and the word for a finger or toe sound alike.
explanation.definitionFit: A digit is any finger or toe, from the Latin word for finger.

clue.text: It's true! Same gets moving and finally becomes an adult

indicators.note: letters that get moving are shifted from their places into a fresh order

blocks.note: the word Same without its last letter, a cut the clue does not signal

explanation.surface: An insistence that someone is growing up at last.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is loose: TRUE and SAME together have an extra E beyond what the answer needs, so Same loses its final E though nothing in the clue says so.
explanation.definitionFit: To mature is to grow up and reach full development, as a child does in becoming an adult.

clue.text: Discounts to be had on broken beaters

indicators.note: something broken is smashed apart, so the word's letters are put back together in a new order

explanation.surface: A shop sale knocking money off damaged egg whisks.
explanation.definitionFit: Rebates are sums returned or knocked off a price, which is what discounts are.

clue.text: that cure for me not quite ready?

indicators.note: not quite there means a letter short, so one letter is removed from the word
loosely, one word stands in for part of the other by sitting inside it

blocks.note: taken as written, losing its A

explanation.surface: A patient asks whether their treatment is still being prepared.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue opens oddly in lower case, so its first word may have been lost in printing; the deletion and insertion still account for every letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A remedy is a medicine or treatment that relieves or heals an illness, so a cure.

clue.text: More money? Looks good to us!

explanation.surface: Workers welcoming the offer of a pay rise.
explanation.walkthrough: The French word for good is borrowed, as crosswords often do.
explanation.definitionFit: A bonus is extra money paid on top of normal wages, so more money.

clue.text: Protecting someone . when you rattle it like that?

blocks.clueFragment: Protecting someone . when you rattle it like that?
blocks.note: surface reading: soothing someone with a baby's rattle
setter's reading: an adjective for acting as a guardian; the rest of the clue is a loose gloss

explanation.surface: Shaking a rattle to calm and guard a small child.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is clear but the role of the rattle half is unclear in the printed clue, so this answer rests on its crossings.
explanation.definitionFit: Tutelar describes a guardian or protector, as in a tutelar deity watching over a place.

clue.text: You are so sly! Gruff and grumpy too!

indicators.note: loosely, the second phrase is so placed that it wraps round the first

blocks.note: text-style shorthand: U for you, R for are

explanation.surface: An accusation that someone is both cunning and bad-tempered.
explanation.walkthrough: U and R stand for the sounds of 'you' and 'are', a long-standing crossword shorthand.
explanation.definitionFit: Surly means bad-tempered and unfriendly, both gruff and grumpy.

clue.text: There's always time to take the rap in the priesthood

definitions.note: a phrase for someone holding high rank among the clergy, standing in for a noun

explanation.surface: A cleric with endless time on their hands ends up taking the blame.
explanation.walkthrough: TIME taking in RAP, rearranged, spells PRIMATE; the clue prints no clear signal for the shuffle, so this parse is loose.
explanation.definitionFit: A primate is an archbishop or senior bishop, the top rank of a country's clergy.

clue.text: Teacher's pet or just a creep?

blocks.note: first meaning: a pupil given duties by the teacher
second meaning: a large lizard, a creature that creeps along

explanation.walkthrough: 'Creep' looks like an insult for a sycophantic pupil; here it means a creeping animal, the monitor lizard.
explanation.definitionFit: A class monitor is a favoured pupil given small duties, and a monitor is also a big lizard that crawls.

clue.text: I go for butter! How's that for a testimony?

indicators.note: to have a go at something is to work it over, so these letters are worked into a new order

explanation.surface: An enthusiastic endorsement of butter, offered like an advertising testimonial.
explanation.definitionFit: A tribute is a statement or gift showing praise and esteem, much as a testimonial is.

clue.text: What a show! Sid returns to find it being acted out

indicators.note: something that returns heads back the way it came, so this name is read from its end

blocks.note: a play is a story acted out on stage

explanation.surface: Sid comes back to the theatre and is delighted by the performance.
explanation.definitionFit: A display is an exhibition or spectacle put on for people to look at, a show.

clue.text: It's such a majestic time of the year!

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as praise for one season; the word is both an adjective for grandeur and the name of a month.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective stressed on its second syllable it means grand or venerable; as a proper noun it names the calendar month.

clue.text: Moves in circles which I try for ages to do

blocks.clueFragment: Moves in circles which I try for ages to do
blocks.note: surface reading: someone struggling to get into a social set
setter's reading: physically spins round and round

explanation.surface: A social climber who has tried for years to mix with the right people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moves in circles' sounds like belonging to a social set; it means turning round and round. The tail of the clue only dresses up the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: To gyrate is to revolve or spin around a centre, moving in circles.

clue.text: He gets Arthur to begin at the fireside

indicators.note: only the opening part of the name is used, the rest is dropped

blocks.note: the first four letters of the name

explanation.surface: A man is joined by Arthur as they settle down beside the fire.
explanation.definitionFit: The hearth is the floor of a fireplace, and by extension the fireside and home.

clue.text: Would have the last word!

blocks.note: surface reading: someone who always wins arguments
setter's reading: the final words written about a person, on their gravestone

explanation.walkthrough: Having the last word sounds like winning an argument; here it is literally the last thing said of someone, carved on the grave.
explanation.definitionFit: An epitaph is the inscription on a tomb, the final words said about the dead.

clue.text: Gets a lift and sees most of his etchings

indicators.note: most of means not all, so the end of the word is cut away

blocks.note: the word with its ending trimmed

explanation.surface: A man accepts a lift home and is shown the driver's etchings.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface nods to the old line 'come up and see my etchings'. No shuffle signal is printed, so the rearrangement is loose.
explanation.definitionFit: To hitch is to hitchhike, travelling by free rides from passing drivers, so getting a lift.

clue.text: How it changes when Walter's beheaded

definitions.note: a phrase standing for the verb 'changes'

indicators.note: losing its head means the word loses its first letter

blocks.note: the name with its possessive, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A grim question about what happens after poor Walter's execution.
explanation.definitionFit: To alter is to change or modify, so it is what something does when it changes.

clue.text: Keep calm, Rae my sweet!

blocks.note: the girl's name, taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone soothing an upset sweetheart called Rae.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My sweet' reads as an endearment for Rae, but sweet is the definition. The letters of CALM and RAE rearrange with no clear signal printed for the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: Caramel is a chewy confection of cooked sugar and butter, a sweet.

clue.text: Something to sing about — a vehicle that requires only %ids of the oil!

indicators.note: the scan's %ids is two thirds, so of a three-letter word only two letters are kept and one thrown away

blocks.note: a car is a road vehicle
the word with its middle letter dropped

explanation.surface: A boast about a car so economical it needs only part of its oil.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed '%ids' is a scanning error for two-thirds: two of the three letters of the word oil are kept.
explanation.definitionFit: A carol is a joyful song, especially one sung at Christmas, something to sing.

clue.text: Craze taken up by Ian and his mother

indicators.note: loosely, letters taken up and set down again land in a new order

blocks.note: ma is an informal word for mother

explanation.surface: A new fad embraced by Ian and his mum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taken up' wants to read the name backwards in a down clue, but that gives NAI; only a rearrangement of IAN with MA fits.
explanation.definitionFit: A mania is an intense enthusiasm shared by many people, a craze.

clue.text: How that Alvin does his block!

indicators.note: asking how something is done hints at a way of rearranging, so the name is reordered

explanation.surface: Admiring how Alvin carves his block of wood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Block' sounds like a block of wood or a mental block; it is the smith's iron block.
explanation.definitionFit: An anvil is the heavy iron block on which a blacksmith hammers metal into shape.

clue.text: I can't take it! It's gone down!

explanation.surface: Someone at the end of their tether, and then something sinks.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of I CANT with IT rearrange to the answer; no shuffle signal is printed, so the parse is loose. The famous liner sank in 1912.
explanation.definitionFit: The Titanic is the ocean liner that went down on her maiden voyage, so she is the ship that has gone down.

clue.text: A way to reunite — go by train

indicators.note: a way of doing something suggests another arrangement, so the letters are put in a different order

explanation.surface: Advice that taking the train is a good way to get people back together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Train' looks like the railway; it is a train of followers.
explanation.definitionFit: A retinue is the group of attendants following an important person, also called a train.

clue.text: Lee takes a trip and meets someone like 9 across!

explanation.surface: Lee goes on holiday and runs into a creep.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of LEE and TRIP rearrange; the clue prints no separate shuffle signal, so 'takes a trip' does double duty. 9 across is the monitor, a lizard.
explanation.definitionFit: A monitor lizard is a reptile, so a reptile is something of the same kind as the 9 across answer.

clue.text: Those rascals are going out with some Oriental sailors

indicators.note: going out on the town suggests getting mixed up, so these letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: Some scoundrels head out for the night with a group of sailors.
explanation.definitionFit: Lascars were seamen from India and Southeast Asia who crewed European ships.
